title: U.S. government urges judge to keep alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator locked up
summary: The U.S. government is pushing for the alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator to stay behind bars. He argues Melody Bryant knew perfectly well that the shooter planned to commit a mass…

image.caption: Melody Bryant, who is charged under the name James Cody Bryant, is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country. (Lois Silver)

blocks.text: British Columbia

The U.S. government is pushing for the alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator to stay behind bars. He argues Melody Bryant knew perfectly well that the shooter planned to commit a mass atrocity, and took concrete steps to further that plan.
Accused 'knew perfectly well' shooter planned mass atrocity, took concrete steps to help, court filing says

In a new court filing, an Assistant United States Attorney says the alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator knew "perfectly well" Jesse Van Rootselaar planned to commit a mass atrocity, and took multiple, concrete steps to further that plan.

Last week, Melody Bryant, 30, who is charged under the name James Cody Bryant, filed a motion asking a Seattle District Court judge to review and revoke a previous detention order that is keeping her behind bars.
The U.S. government opposes the motion, saying Bryant poses a danger to the public if freed.

"A defendant whose character allows them to help plan a mass shooting, and then sits back and (literally) tries to watch as schoolchildren are murdered instead of 'snitching' on the killer, is a danger to the community and should be detained pending trial," wrote Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Greenberg in a 19-page response.

blocks.text: Bryant is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, an offence that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $250,000 US fine. She has pleaded not guilty. The trial is scheduled to begin Dec. 6, 2027.
Bryant is seeking a conditional release and claims she believed the shooter's plans were just a “fantasy” — a notion the government calls "bogus."

The government's response reiterates allegations in its criminal complaint, that Bryant's action made her a conspirator in the mass shooting. Those actions, the complaint says, include providing money for the shooter to purchase items to use in the attack, giving tactical advice, agreeing to livestream the event and agreeing not to report the plot to law enforcement.

Eight people were killed in the Feb. 10, 2026, mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, including five children, an educational assistant, and the shooter's mother and half-brother, both pictured bottom right. (CBC News)
On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother Jennifer Strang, 39, and half-brother Emmett Jacobs, 11, in their home.

She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she gunned down Abel Mwansa Jr., 12, Zoey Benoit, 12, Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Kylie Smith, 12, Ticaria Lampert, 12, and educational assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39.
Two other students were shot but survived.

The U.S. government says as the murders were unfolding, Bryant was in direct communication with Van Rootselaar, who was sitting in a vehicle after killing her mother and half-brother "about to drive to the Tumbler Ridge school to carry out more murders."

blocks.text: Bryant knew what was happening and chose to help Van Rootselaar, who didn't know how to drive, figure out how to start the car, the court filing says.
"During this entire conversation, Bryant knew full well that 'violence was imminent' and chose to further it," wrote Greenberg.

He says the evidence against Bryant is "extremely strong" and is based primarily on her own words in conversations with Van Rootselaar. He adds her actions placed a higher value on loyalty to, and affection for, Van Rootselaar than on saving the lives of innocent children.

Jesse Van Rootselaar sent this photo of an unfinished improvised explosive device she was building to Melody Bryant on Jan. 22, 2026. An Assistant United States Attorney says the device is notably lacking a lighter, which Bryant is alleged to have sent money to Van Rootselaar to purchase. (Assistant United States Attorney)
Bryant wanted to engage in violence, gov't says

The government's response highlights a conversation between Bryant and Van Rootselaar less than a month before the mass shooting, in which Bryant "discussed the desire to engage in violence, specifically a stabbing."
Bryant said she planned to get a gun for self defense because she would enjoy it less than "digging a knife into flesh," and would "feel less likely to enjoy using it."
"I just feel like there's something to enjoy about how direct you are in their maiming. Warm blood getting on your hands. Any movement being agony," wrote Bryant.

The U.S. government says Bryant's alleged crimes were mainly committed through online communications, and it would be difficult to adequately monitor her if she were to be released. It notes Bryant has two roommates with access to numerous electronic devices in the home, including at least five computers, a smart TV, four online gaming devices, and several other gaming consoles.
"Releasing Bryant under these circumstances is too big of a risk to take with the safety of the community."
